questions.q: On the Fourth of July, we celebrate America's...
questions.explain: The Fourth of July is America's birthday. People have parades, picnics and fireworks.
questions.tip: Fireworks go boom for America's birthday party!

questions.q: What lights up the sky on the Fourth of July?
questions.explain: Many towns shoot colorful fireworks into the night sky on the Fourth of July.
questions.tip: Pop, sparkle, boom: fireworks are the birthday candles for America!

questions.q: Thanksgiving is a day to say...
questions.explain: On Thanksgiving, families share a meal and say thank you for the good things they have.
questions.tip: Thanks-giving means giving thanks!

questions.q: What food do many families eat on Thanksgiving?
questions.explain: Many families eat turkey, along with foods like corn, potatoes and pie.
questions.tip: Gobble, gobble, it's turkey time!

questions.q: On Martin Luther King Jr. Day, we remember a man who wanted all people to be treated...
questions.explain: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. worked so that all people would be treated fairly and kindly.
questions.tip: Dr. King had a dream that everyone would be treated the same.

questions.q: Veterans Day is a day to thank people who served in the...
questions.explain: Veterans are people who served in the army, navy, air force, marines or other military groups.
questions.tip: Veterans helped keep our country safe, so we say thank you.

questions.q: Presidents' Day honors our country's...
questions.explain: Presidents' Day remembers leaders of our country, like George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.
questions.tip: Presidents' Day is the presidents' special day!

questions.q: Long ago, there were no cars. What did people ride?
questions.explain: Long ago, people rode horses or rode in wagons pulled by horses.
questions.tip: Clip-clop, clip-clop: that was the sound of long-ago travel.

questions.q: Long ago, there were no electric lights. What did people use at night?
questions.explain: People used candles and oil lamps to see in the dark.
questions.tip: Flicker, flicker, little flame, long ago you lit the way.

questions.q: Which toy is from long, long ago?
questions.explain: Long ago, kids played with simple toys like wooden tops, dolls and balls.
questions.tip: Spin a top, no plug, no stop!

questions.q: Long ago, there were no phones. How did people send a message far away?
questions.explain: People wrote letters on paper, and the letters were carried to far away places.
questions.tip: Paper, pen, and wait for the reply: that was long-ago texting!

questions.q: Is a computer something new or something from very long ago?
questions.explain: Computers are new. Your great-great-grandparents did not have them when they were little.
questions.tip: If it plugs in or has a screen, it's probably new.

questions.q: Long ago, how did people wash clothes?
questions.explain: Long ago, people scrubbed clothes by hand in a tub of water.
questions.tip: Scrub-a-dub-dub, clothes in a tub!

questions.q: What colors are on the American flag?
questions.explain: The American flag is red, white and blue, with stars and stripes.
questions.tip: Red, white and blue, the flag waves for you!

questions.q: What shapes are on the American flag?
questions.explain: The flag has white stars on a blue box and red and white stripes.
questions.tip: People call the flag the Stars and Stripes!

questions.q: The bald eagle is a symbol of America. What kind of animal is it?
questions.explain: The bald eagle is a big bird with a white head. It is America's national bird.
questions.tip: The eagle is not really bald; its white feathers just look like a bald head!

questions.q: The Statue of Liberty holds something up high in her hand. What is it?
questions.explain: The Statue of Liberty holds up a torch, like a light welcoming people.
questions.tip: Lady Liberty lifts her light up high to say hello!

questions.q: The Liberty Bell is a famous bell. What does it have?
questions.explain: The Liberty Bell has a big crack in it, so it is not rung anymore.
questions.tip: Crack goes the bell, and that's the story people tell!

questions.q: Who lives and works in the White House?
questions.explain: The White House is where the President of the United States lives and works.
questions.tip: The White House is the President's house, painted white!

prek.name: My Family and Town Long Ago

questions.q: Your grandma and grandpa were once little kids too. Was that long ago?
questions.explain: Grandparents were children many years ago, a long time before you were born.
questions.tip: Ask Grandma: what did you play when you were little?

questions.q: Where can you go to see very old things?
questions.explain: A museum keeps old and special things so people can see them and learn.
questions.tip: Museums are treasure boxes for old things!

questions.q: What can show us how people looked long ago?
questions.explain: Old photos show how people dressed and what places looked like long ago.
questions.tip: Old photos are little windows into the past.

questions.q: A birthday celebrates the day you were...
questions.explain: Your birthday is the day you were born. Each year it comes back and you get one year older.
questions.tip: Birth-day: the day of your birth!

questions.q: Which happened first: you were a baby, or you are big now?
questions.explain: Everyone is a baby first, then grows bigger. That is your own history!
questions.tip: First tiny, then tall: that's how we grow!

questions.q: Yesterday is the day before today. Is yesterday in the past?
questions.explain: Yesterday already happened, so it is in the past. History is all about the past.
questions.tip: Yesterday is gone, today is here, tomorrow is coming near.

questions.q: Independence Day on July 4th celebrates the Declaration of Independence from 1776. What did it say?
questions.say: Independence Day on July fourth celebrates the Declaration of Independence from seventeen seventy-six. What did it say?
choices: America would be free from Britain
questions.explain: On July 4, 1776, American leaders said the colonies were free and independent from Great Britain.
questions.tip: Seventeen seventy-six, the year the colonies said we're free, what a fix!

questions.q: Who shared a harvest feast together in 1621 that we remember at Thanksgiving?
questions.say: Who shared a harvest feast together in sixteen twenty-one that we remember at Thanksgiving?
questions.explain: The Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people shared a harvest feast in 1621 in Plymouth.
questions.tip: Pilgrims and Wampanoag, sharing food together: that's the Thanksgiving story.

questions.q: Presidents' Day comes in February, near the birthdays of which two presidents?
questions.explain: Washington was born on February 22 and Lincoln on February 12, so both birthdays are in February.
questions.tip: February has two famous birthdays: Abe and George, on the penny and the quarter!

questions.q: Labor Day is a holiday that honors...
questions.explain: Labor means work. Labor Day honors working people and is in September.
questions.tip: Labor means work, so on Labor Day workers get a rest!

questions.q: Memorial Day is a day to remember...
choices: Soldiers who died serving our country
questions.explain: On Memorial Day, in May, we remember members of the military who gave their lives for the country.
questions.tip: Memorial sounds like memory: it's a day to remember.

questions.q: Veterans Day is on November 11. Who does it honor?
questions.say: Veterans Day is on November eleventh. Who does it honor?
choices: Everyone who served in the military
questions.explain: Veterans Day thanks all people who have served in the military, living or not.
questions.tip: Eleven-eleven: November 11 is the day we thank veterans.

questions.q: Martin Luther King Jr. Day honors a leader who worked for...
questions.explain: Dr. King worked peacefully so that people of all colors would be treated equally.
questions.tip: Dr. King said 'I have a dream' of fairness for everyone.

questions.q: Flag Day is in June. What does it celebrate?
questions.explain: Flag Day, on June 14, celebrates the day in 1777 when the stars and stripes was picked as the flag.
questions.tip: Flag Day: the flag gets its very own day!

questions.q: Long ago, many children went to school in one room with kids of all ages. What was it called?
questions.explain: In a one-room schoolhouse, one teacher taught children of many ages together.
questions.tip: One room, one teacher, all the kids: big and little learned together.

questions.q: Before refrigerators, what kept food cold?
choices: An icebox with a block of ice
questions.explain: An icebox held a big block of ice that kept food cold until it melted.
questions.tip: Icebox: a box with ice, how nice!

questions.q: Who made the first powered airplane flight in 1903?
questions.say: Who made the first powered airplane flight in nineteen oh three?
questions.explain: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew the first powered airplane at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903.
questions.tip: The Wright brothers got flying right!

questions.q: Who is famous for inventing the telephone?
questions.explain: Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for the telephone in 1876.
questions.tip: Ring, ring goes the Bell: Alexander Graham Bell!

questions.q: Thomas Edison is famous for his work on which invention?
questions.explain: Thomas Edison and his team made a light bulb that could glow for a long time.
questions.tip: Picture a light bulb over Edison's head: a bright idea!

questions.q: The Pony Express carried mail across the West. How did it travel?
questions.explain: Pony Express riders raced on horses, swapping for fresh horses along the way, to carry mail in 1860 and 1861.
questions.tip: Pony Express: the mail came by pony, fast as you can guess!

questions.q: Long ago, people wrote with feathers dipped in ink. What were these called?
questions.explain: A quill pen was made from a bird feather. Writers dipped it in ink again and again.
questions.tip: A quill is a feather that writes: tickle and scribble!

questions.q: Long ago, how did people cook food at home?
choices: Over a fire or on a wood stove
questions.explain: People cooked in a fireplace or on a stove that burned wood.
questions.tip: Long ago dinner was cooked by fire, sizzling higher and higher!

questions.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
questions.explain: France gave the Statue of Liberty as a gift of friendship. It stands in New York Harbor.
questions.tip: Lady Liberty is a French friend in New York!

questions.q: How many stars are on the American flag today?
questions.explain: There is one star for each of the 50 states.
questions.tip: Fifty stars for fifty states: one star for each state!

questions.q: The 13 stripes on the flag stand for...
questions.say: The thirteen stripes on the flag stand for...
questions.explain: The 13 stripes stand for the 13 colonies that became the first states.
questions.tip: Stars are for states now; stripes are for the starting thirteen.

questions.q: Mount Rushmore has the faces of how many presidents carved in stone?
questions.explain: Mount Rushmore in South Dakota shows Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln.
questions.tip: Four faces in a mountain: like a giant stone family photo!

questions.q: What is the name of America's national anthem?
questions.explain: The Star-Spangled Banner is the national anthem. A banner is a flag, and spangled means covered in sparkles.
questions.tip: Star-spangled banner means a flag covered with stars!

questions.q: In which city is the Liberty Bell?
questions.explain: The Liberty Bell is in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where the Declaration of Independence was signed.
questions.tip: Philadelphia means city of brotherly love, and it's home to the Liberty Bell.

questions.q: The Pledge of Allegiance is a promise to be loyal to...
choices: The flag and the United States
questions.explain: When people say the Pledge of Allegiance, they promise loyalty to the flag and the country.
questions.tip: Pledge means promise: hand on heart, say it from the start.

questions.q: Which tall man in a star-covered hat is a symbol of the United States?
questions.explain: Uncle Sam, with his top hat and white beard, is a cartoon symbol of the United States.
questions.tip: Uncle Sam has the same first letters as United States: U.S.!

questions.q: In what city is the White House?
questions.explain: The White House is in Washington, D.C., the capital of the United States.
questions.tip: D.C. is the capital, and the President lives there; that's easy to see!

questions.q: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.explain: George Washington was the first President. He is on the one-dollar bill and the quarter.
questions.tip: Washington was number one, and he's on the one-dollar bill!

questions.q: Abraham Lincoln was President during which war?
questions.explain: Lincoln led the country during the Civil War and worked to end slavery.
questions.tip: Honest Abe kept the country together during the Civil War.

questions.q: Who flew a kite in a storm to learn about electricity?
questions.explain: Benjamin Franklin did experiments with a kite to show that lightning is electricity.
questions.tip: Ben's kite plus lightning bright equals an electric delight!

questions.q: Rosa Parks is famous for refusing to give up her seat on a...
questions.explain: In 1955, Rosa Parks bravely refused to give up her bus seat, which helped start a fight for fair laws.
questions.tip: Rosa Parks stayed seated so things would be fair for all.

questions.q: Harriet Tubman led many enslaved people to freedom on the...
questions.explain: The Underground Railroad was a secret network of routes and safe houses, not a real railroad.
questions.tip: Harriet was a conductor on a train you could not see!

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.explain: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on July 20, 1969.
questions.tip: Neil took one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.

questions.q: Sacagawea helped which explorers travel across the West?
questions.explain: Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, helped guide and translate for Lewis and Clark.
questions.tip: Sacagawea is on a gold-colored dollar coin, carrying her baby!

questions.q: Amelia Earhart was famous for being a brave...
questions.explain: In 1932, Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly alone across the Atlantic Ocean.
questions.tip: Amelia took to the air: Earhart, air-heart!

questions.q: Johnny Appleseed is remembered for planting lots of...
questions.explain: John Chapman, called Johnny Appleseed, planted apple trees across the Midwest.
questions.tip: His name tells you: Johnny Apple-SEED!

questions.q: A line that shows events in the order they happened is called a...
questions.explain: A timeline puts events in order from first to last.
questions.tip: A timeline is a line of time: first, next, last, in a row!

questions.q: What do we call a person who studies the past?
questions.explain: A historian finds clues about the past and tells its story.
questions.tip: History plus -ian: a historian is a history detective!

questions.q: A chart that shows your parents, grandparents and great-grandparents is a...
questions.explain: A family tree shows how the people in a family are connected over time.
questions.tip: Grandparents are the roots and you are a new leaf!

questions.q: Which comes first?
questions.explain: Yesterday comes before today, and tomorrow comes after today.
questions.tip: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: past, now, next.

questions.q: An old letter written by your great-grandma can help you learn about...
questions.explain: Old letters, diaries and photos are clues about how people lived long ago.
questions.tip: Old letters are time machines made of paper!

questions.q: The past means things that...
questions.explain: The past is everything that already happened. The future is what has not happened yet.
questions.tip: Past is passed: it already went by!

questions.q: How many years are in a century?
questions.explain: A century is 100 years. A decade is 10 years.
questions.tip: A cent is one hundredth of a dollar, and a century is one hundred years!

questions.q: Long ago, how did many towns get started?
choices: Near rivers, roads or good farmland
questions.explain: People settled near water, farmland and roads so they could drink, farm, travel and trade.
questions.tip: Towns grow where water flows!

questions.q: What do we call the people who lived in America first, long before anyone came from Europe?
questions.explain: Native Americans lived in the Americas for thousands of years before Europeans arrived.
questions.tip: Native means from a place: Native Americans were here first.

questions.q: Which direction is at the top of most maps?
questions.explain: Most maps put north at the top, south at the bottom, east on the right and west on the left.
questions.tip: Going around clockwise from the top: Never Eat Soggy Waffles, for North, East, South, West.

questions.q: What does a map key tell you?
questions.explain: The key, also called a legend, explains the little pictures and colors on a map.
questions.tip: The map key unlocks the map's secret pictures.

questions.q: What does a compass rose on a map show?
questions.explain: A compass rose shows which way is north, south, east and west.
questions.tip: A compass rose points the way: N, E, S, W.

questions.q: On a map, what does blue usually show?
questions.explain: Mapmakers use blue for oceans, lakes and rivers.
questions.tip: Blue like the sea.

questions.q: A globe is a model of Earth. What shape is it?
questions.explain: A globe is round like a ball, because Earth is round. That shape is called a sphere.
questions.tip: Earth is round like a ball, and so is a globe.

questions.q: Which one is a continent?
questions.explain: Africa is one of the 7 continents. Texas is a state, Paris is a city, and Canada is a country.
questions.tip: Continents are the biggest pieces of land on Earth.

questions.q: How many continents are there?
questions.explain: There are 7 continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.
questions.tip: 7 continents, like the 7 days of the week.

questions.q: Which one is a landform?
questions.explain: A landform is a natural shape of the land, like a mountain, hill, valley or plain.
questions.tip: Land plus form: the shape the land takes.

questions.q: Which body of water is the biggest?
questions.explain: Oceans are the biggest bodies of water. They cover most of Earth's surface.
questions.tip: Pond, lake, ocean: big, bigger, BIGGEST.

questions.q: Which ocean is along the east coast of the United States?
questions.explain: The Atlantic Ocean is on the east coast. The Pacific Ocean is on the west coast.
questions.tip: The Pilgrims sailed across the Atlantic to reach the East Coast.

questions.q: In what year did Christopher Columbus first sail across the Atlantic to the Americas?
questions.explain: Columbus sailed in 1492 and reached islands in the Caribbean.
questions.tip: In fourteen hundred ninety-two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue.

questions.q: Which country paid for Columbus's first voyage?
questions.explain: King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain paid for the voyage, even though Columbus was born in Genoa.
questions.tip: Columbus sailed for Spain, but his home was Genoa: born in Italy, paid in Spain.

questions.q: What were the names of Columbus's three ships?
questions.explain: Columbus sailed with the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria.
questions.tip: Nina, Pinta, Santa Maria: say it like a little song!

questions.q: Around the year 1000, which Viking explorer reached North America?
questions.explain: Leif Erikson, a Norse explorer, reached North America about 500 years before Columbus.
questions.tip: Leif leaped first: a Viking beat Columbus by about 500 years.

questions.q: Whose expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world?
questions.explain: Magellan's expedition left Spain in 1519. Magellan died in the Philippines, and Juan Sebastian Elcano led the last ship home in 1522.
questions.tip: Magellan's crew made the first full loop around the map: Magellan, the round-the-world man.

questions.q: What were many European explorers hoping to find by sailing west?
choices: A sea route to Asia for spices and silk
A path to the North Pole
questions.explain: Spices and silk from Asia were valuable, and explorers wanted a faster ocean route to get them.
questions.tip: Explorers followed their noses: spices smelled like money!

questions.q: Which Portuguese explorer was the first European to reach India by sailing around Africa?
questions.explain: Vasco da Gama sailed around the southern tip of Africa and reached India in 1498.
questions.tip: Vasco da Gama went around Africa, the long way to India's door.

questions.q: Ponce de Leon explored and named which present-day U.S. state?
questions.explain: In 1513 Ponce de Leon reached and named Florida. A legend says he was looking for a Fountain of Youth.
questions.tip: Florida means flowery: Ponce found flowers, not the Fountain of Youth.

questions.q: Henry Hudson has which river in New York named after him?
questions.explain: Henry Hudson explored the Hudson River in 1609 while sailing for the Dutch.
questions.tip: Hudson's name floats right down the Hudson River!

questions.q: Which Spanish conquistador conquered the Aztec Empire in Mexico?
questions.explain: Hernan Cortes and his allies defeated the Aztec Empire by 1521. Pizarro later conquered the Inca in Peru.
questions.tip: Cortes for the Aztecs, Pizarro for the Peru Inca: P goes with P.

questions.q: Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River for which country?
questions.explain: Cartier's voyages in the 1530s helped France claim land in what is now Canada.
questions.tip: Jacques is a French name, and Cartier claimed Canada for France.

questions.q: What was the first permanent English settlement in North America?
questions.explain: Jamestown, Virginia, was founded in 1607.
questions.tip: Jamestown came first, sixteen-oh-seven: J for Jamestown, J for 'just the beginning'.

questions.q: In what year did the Pilgrims sail on the Mayflower and found Plymouth?
questions.explain: The Pilgrims arrived in 1620 and founded Plymouth Colony in Massachusetts.
questions.tip: Sixteen-twenty, Mayflower full of plenty (of seasick Pilgrims)!

questions.q: What was the Mayflower Compact?
choices: An agreement to make fair laws and govern themselves
A list of foods on the ship
questions.explain: Before landing, the Pilgrims signed the Mayflower Compact, agreeing to make and follow laws for the good of the colony.
questions.tip: Compact means a promise packed tight: we'll rule together right.

questions.q: How many English colonies joined together to become the first United States?
questions.explain: The 13 colonies along the Atlantic coast became the first 13 states.
questions.tip: Count the stripes on the flag: 13 colonies!

questions.q: Which Wampanoag man spoke English and helped the Pilgrims learn to plant corn?
questions.explain: Squanto had been to England and could speak English, so he helped the Pilgrims farm and fish.
questions.tip: Squanto showed them to bury a fish with the corn seeds for fertilizer: fishy farming!

questions.q: Pocahontas was the daughter of a Powhatan leader near which colony?
questions.explain: Pocahontas was the daughter of Powhatan, a powerful leader near Jamestown, Virginia.
questions.tip: Pocahontas and Powhatan both start with P, near Jamestown in Virginia.

questions.q: Who founded the colony of Pennsylvania?
questions.explain: William Penn founded Pennsylvania in the 1680s as a place of religious freedom, especially for Quakers.
questions.tip: Penn-sylvania means Penn's woods!

questions.q: Which crop made the Virginia colony money?
questions.explain: Tobacco grew well in Virginia and was sold to England, making the colony rich.
questions.tip: Virginia's money grew in the field as tobacco leaves.

questions.q: The New England colonies were known for fishing, shipbuilding and...
choices: Rocky soil that made farming hard
questions.explain: New England had cold winters and rocky soil, so many people turned to the sea for work.
questions.tip: New England: rocks in the fields, so they went fishing for meals.

questions.q: Which was the last of the 13 colonies to be founded?
questions.explain: Georgia was founded in 1732 by James Oglethorpe.
questions.tip: G is for Georgia, the colony that came at the end of the line.

questions.q: Colonists who were angry about British taxes used which slogan?
choices: Give me pizza or give me pie
questions.explain: Colonists said it was unfair to be taxed by Parliament when they had no representatives there.
questions.tip: No vote, no tax: if we don't have a say, we won't pay!

questions.q: In 1773, colonists dumped tea into Boston Harbor to protest a tax. What is this called?
questions.explain: On December 16, 1773, colonists threw 342 chests of tea into the harbor.
questions.tip: Some party: nobody drank the tea, but the fish got a giant cup!

questions.q: Which 1765 tax made colonists pay for printed papers like newspapers?
questions.explain: The Stamp Act required a tax stamp on newspapers, legal papers and even playing cards.
questions.tip: Stamp Act: colonists stamped their feet about stamps on paper!

questions.q: Who rode at night in 1775 to warn that British troops were coming?
questions.explain: On April 18, 1775, Paul Revere and other riders warned colonists that British soldiers were marching.
questions.tip: One if by land, two if by sea: Revere had lanterns hung to signal patriots across the river.

questions.q: Where were the first battles of the American Revolution fought in 1775?
questions.explain: The war began at Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts on April 19, 1775.
questions.tip: L and C start the war: Lexington, Concord, and the shot heard round the world.

questions.q: Who was the main writer of the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft, and Congress adopted it on July 4, 1776.
questions.tip: Jefferson's pen made the Declaration: J for July and Jefferson.

questions.q: Who led the Continental Army during the Revolution?
questions.explain: George Washington commanded the American army and later became the first President.
questions.tip: Washington was the general first, then the President: always number one.

questions.q: Who was the king of Great Britain during the American Revolution?
questions.explain: King George III ruled Great Britain from 1760 to 1820.
questions.tip: George vs. George: King George III against General George Washington!

questions.q: Where did Washington's army spend the hard winter of 1777 to 1778?
questions.explain: At Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, soldiers suffered from cold and hunger but trained and grew stronger.
questions.tip: Valley Forge forged the army: cold as ice but tough as iron.

questions.q: Which country became an important ally and helped the Americans win?
questions.explain: After the American win at Saratoga in 1777, France sent soldiers, ships and money.
questions.tip: France said oui to helping the U.S.!

questions.q: Where did the British army surrender in 1781, effectively ending the fighting?
questions.explain: British General Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown in 1781. The Treaty of Paris in 1783 officially ended the war.
questions.tip: Yorktown: you're done, the war is won!

questions.q: Which Founding Father invented bifocal glasses and the lightning rod?
questions.explain: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, writer, scientist and inventor.
questions.tip: Ben's on the $100 bill, and he had a hundred ideas!

questions.q: Which President bought the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803?
questions.explain: Jefferson's Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States.
questions.tip: Jefferson's big buy doubled the country: a two-for-one deal!

questions.q: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery and became famous as a...
questions.explain: Frederick Douglass wrote books and gave powerful speeches to end slavery.
questions.tip: Douglass's words were his tools: he spoke and wrote for freedom.

questions.q: Susan B. Anthony worked hard for women's right to...
questions.explain: Susan B. Anthony was a leader in the fight for women's suffrage, the right to vote.
questions.tip: Susan B. said women should be able to vote: B for ballot!

questions.q: Clara Barton, a nurse during the Civil War, founded which group?
questions.explain: Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross in 1881 to help people in war and disasters.
questions.tip: Clara cares, and the Red Cross is there!

questions.q: George Washington Carver found hundreds of uses for which plant?
questions.explain: Carver, a scientist, found many uses for peanuts and sweet potatoes and taught farmers to rotate crops.
questions.tip: Carver was nuts about peanuts!

questions.q: In 1947, Jackie Robinson became the first Black player in modern Major League Baseball. Which team did he play for?
questions.explain: Jackie Robinson joined the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947. Every player in MLB now wears his number 42 on Jackie Robinson Day.
questions.tip: Number 42 broke through!

questions.q: Which President is famous for protecting nature and creating national parks and forests?
questions.explain: Theodore Roosevelt protected millions of acres of land. The teddy bear is named after him.
questions.tip: Teddy Roosevelt loved the outdoors, and the teddy bear is named for him!

questions.q: Which document did Abraham Lincoln issue in 1863 to declare enslaved people in Confederate states free?
questions.explain: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on January 1, 1863.
questions.tip: Emancipate means to set free: Lincoln's proclamation of liberty.

questions.q: Who became the first African American justice on the U.S. Supreme Court?
questions.explain: Thurgood Marshall joined the Supreme Court in 1967 after winning Brown v. Board of Education as a lawyer.
questions.tip: Thurgood was a good lawyer and a great judge.

questions.q: What is the capital of the United States?
questions.explain: Washington, D.C. has been the capital since 1800. D.C. stands for District of Columbia.
questions.tip: The capital is named for the first President: Washington!

questions.q: On which coast were the 13 colonies?
questions.explain: The colonies stretched along the Atlantic Ocean from New Hampshire to Georgia.
questions.tip: The colonies faced England across the Atlantic: East for the start of the feast.

questions.q: Lewis and Clark traveled up which river at the start of their journey west?
questions.explain: Starting in 1804, the Corps of Discovery paddled up the Missouri River toward the Rocky Mountains.
questions.tip: Lewis and Clark said 'Show me the way!' up the Missouri, the Show-Me State's river.

questions.q: From which country did the United States buy Alaska in 1867?
questions.explain: Secretary of State William Seward arranged the purchase. Critics called it Seward's Folly, but Alaska proved very valuable.
questions.tip: Russia is just across a narrow strait from Alaska: a next-door sale!

questions.q: Which was the 50th state to join the United States, in 1959?
questions.explain: Alaska became the 49th state and Hawaii the 50th, both in 1959.
questions.tip: Alaska came first and Hawaii last: snow then surf in 1959.

questions.q: Delaware is nicknamed The First State. Why?
choices: It was the first to approve the Constitution
It was the first colony founded
questions.explain: Delaware ratified the Constitution on December 7, 1787, before any other state.
questions.tip: Delaware didn't delay: first to say yes to the Constitution!

questions.q: In 1848, gold was found in which place, starting a rush of people west?
questions.explain: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill in 1848. Thousands of forty-niners rushed to California in 1849.
questions.tip: San Francisco's football team is the 49ers, named for the gold rushers!

questions.q: Pioneers in covered wagons followed the Oregon Trail to reach...
questions.explain: The Oregon Trail ran about 2,000 miles from Missouri to the Oregon Country.
questions.tip: The Oregon Trail ends in Oregon, just like the name says!

questions.q: The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, connected the Hudson River to which Great Lake?
questions.explain: The Erie Canal linked Albany on the Hudson to Buffalo on Lake Erie, making trade much easier.
questions.tip: Erie Canal goes to Lake Erie: the name gives it away!

questions.q: Which mountains near the East Coast made it hard for early colonists to move west?
questions.explain: The Appalachians run from Canada to Alabama. Daniel Boone helped open a path through the Cumberland Gap.
questions.tip: Appalachians are in the East, Rockies in the West: A comes before R, East before West.

questions.q: Ancient Egypt grew up along which river?
questions.explain: The Nile gave Egypt water, food and a highway for boats.
questions.tip: Without the Nile, Egypt would be all sand and no smile.

questions.q: What was the ruler of ancient Egypt called?
questions.explain: Egyptians believed the pharaoh was a god-king who ruled the land.
questions.tip: Pharaoh rhymes with 'arrow': straight to the top of Egypt!

questions.q: What were the great pyramids built to be?
questions.explain: Pyramids were giant tombs that held pharaohs' bodies and treasures for the afterlife.
questions.tip: Pyramids were pharaoh pillows for the forever sleep.

questions.q: What was ancient Egyptian picture writing called?
questions.explain: Hieroglyphics used hundreds of pictures and symbols to stand for sounds and ideas.
questions.tip: Hieroglyphs were the first emojis carved in stone!

questions.q: Why did Egyptians make mummies?
choices: To preserve bodies for the afterlife
questions.explain: Egyptians believed the body was needed in the afterlife, so they dried and wrapped it carefully.
questions.tip: Wrap it up tight so it lasts for all time!

questions.q: Which stone helped scholars finally read hieroglyphics?
questions.explain: The Rosetta Stone has the same message in hieroglyphics, a later Egyptian script and Greek. Jean-Francois Champollion cracked the code in 1822.
questions.tip: The Rosetta Stone was the answer key to the Egyptian test!

questions.q: What did Egyptians make from a reed plant to write on?
questions.explain: Papyrus was pressed into sheets for writing. The word paper comes from papyrus.
questions.tip: Papyrus sounds like paper because paper's name came from it!

questions.q: In 1922, Howard Carter found the nearly untouched tomb of which young pharaoh?
questions.explain: King Tut's tomb was full of treasures, including his famous gold mask.
questions.tip: King Tut, the boy king, was found with golden bling!

questions.q: The Great Sphinx has the body of a lion and the head of a...
questions.explain: The Great Sphinx at Giza is a huge statue with a lion's body and a human head.
questions.tip: Half lion, half human: the Sphinx is a stone mix-up!

questions.q: Why was the yearly Nile flood good for Egyptian farmers?
choices: It left rich, dark soil for crops
It washed away all the plants
It brought sand to build pyramids
questions.explain: When the flood went down, it left fertile black mud. Egyptians called their land Kemet, the black land.
questions.tip: The flood was the Nile's gift: free fertilizer every year!

questions.q: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for which pharaoh?
questions.explain: The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu about 4,500 years ago. It was the tallest human-made structure for thousands of years.
questions.tip: Khufu's pyramid is so big it makes you go 'Whew, Khufu!'

questions.q: Mesopotamia lay between which two rivers?
questions.explain: Mesopotamia means land between the rivers, in what is now mostly Iraq.
questions.tip: Meso = middle, potamia = rivers (like hippopotamus, the river horse).

questions.q: What was the Sumerian system of wedge-shaped writing called?
questions.explain: Cuneiform was pressed into wet clay tablets with a reed stylus. It is one of the oldest writing systems.
questions.tip: Cunei means wedge: cuneiform is wedge-form writing.

questions.q: The Code of Hammurabi was an early written set of laws from which city?
questions.explain: King Hammurabi of Babylon had about 282 laws carved on a stone pillar around 1750 BC.
questions.tip: Hammurabi hammered his laws into stone so no one could babble they didn't know them.

questions.q: Which phrase is often used to describe the punishments in Hammurabi's Code?
questions.explain: Many punishments matched the crime, and they often depended on a person's social class.
questions.tip: Eye for an eye, tooth for a tooth: Hammurabi's rules were tough as a tooth.

questions.q: What were the large stepped temple towers of Mesopotamia called?
questions.explain: Ziggurats were built of mud brick with a temple on top for the city's god.
questions.tip: A ziggurat zigzags up like giant stairs to the sky.

questions.q: The curved region of rich farmland from Mesopotamia to the Mediterranean is called the...
questions.explain: The Fertile Crescent was one of the first places where people farmed and built cities.
questions.tip: Fertile means good for growing, crescent means moon shape: a growing moon of farms.

questions.q: Which ancient story about a king's search for immortality comes from Mesopotamia?
questions.explain: The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest known works of literature.
questions.tip: Gilgamesh was a king on a quest to never die, but learned that everyone must.

questions.q: Which ruler of Akkad is often called the founder of the world's first empire?
questions.explain: Around 2300 BC, Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian city-states and united them under one ruler.
questions.tip: Sargon was first to the empire game: Sargon, the sarge in charge.

questions.q: The ancient Sumerians are credited with inventing which of these?
questions.explain: Writing developed in Sumer around 3200 BC, first for keeping records of goods and trade.
questions.tip: Writing began as shopping lists: Sumerians counted sheep on clay!

questions.q: Which Greek city-state is known as the birthplace of democracy?
questions.explain: In Athens, male citizens voted directly on laws in an assembly.
questions.tip: Athens was all about voting; Sparta was all about fighting.

questions.q: Which Greek city-state was famous for its strict military training?
questions.explain: Spartan boys began military training at about age seven.
questions.tip: Today 'spartan' means plain and tough, just like Spartan life.

questions.q: What is the Greek word for a city-state?
questions.explain: A polis was a city and its surrounding land with its own government. The words politics and police come from it.
questions.tip: Polis gives us politics, police and metropolis!

questions.q: The ancient Olympic Games were held in honor of which god?
questions.explain: The games at Olympia honored Zeus, king of the gods. Tradition dates the first games to 776 BC.
questions.tip: The games were held at Olympia, Zeus's holy site, so they're the Olympics!

questions.q: Who was the teacher of Alexander the Great?
questions.explain: Aristotle, a student of Plato, tutored the young Alexander in Macedonia.
questions.tip: Socrates taught Plato, Plato taught Aristotle, Aristotle taught Alexander: S-P-A-A, like a SPA for brains.

questions.q: The Parthenon in Athens was a temple to which goddess?
questions.explain: The Parthenon honored Athena, goddess of wisdom and protector of Athens.
questions.tip: Athena watches over Athens: the city even shares her name.

questions.q: Who is traditionally credited with the epic poems the Iliad and the Odyssey?
questions.explain: The Iliad tells of the Trojan War, and the Odyssey tells of Odysseus's long trip home.
questions.tip: Homer's hero heads home: an odyssey is a very long trip, just like Odysseus took.

questions.q: In 490 BC, Athenians defeated the Persians at which battle, later the name of a long race?
questions.explain: Legend says a runner ran from Marathon to Athens with news of the victory.
questions.tip: Run 26.2 miles today and you're honoring the Battle of Marathon!

questions.q: The Peloponnesian War was fought mainly between which two city-states?
questions.explain: The war lasted from 431 to 404 BC and ended with Sparta's victory.
questions.tip: Greeks vs. Greeks: Athens' navy against Sparta's army.

questions.q: Alexander the Great came from which kingdom north of Greece?
questions.explain: Alexander built a huge empire stretching from Greece to Egypt and into India before he died in 323 BC.
questions.tip: Alexander made Macedonia's map mega-sized.

questions.q: According to legend, which twins founded Rome?
questions.explain: The legend says the twins were raised by a she-wolf, and Romulus named the city after himself.
questions.tip: Rome is named for Romulus: Rom- and Rom-!

questions.q: In the Roman Republic, the two top elected officials were called...
questions.explain: Two consuls served one-year terms so no single person held all the power.
questions.tip: Two consuls to counsel: no one gets to rule alone.

questions.q: Julius Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March in which year?
questions.explain: A group of senators stabbed Caesar on March 15, 44 BC.
questions.tip: Beware the Ides of March: March 15th, 44 BC.

questions.q: Who became the first Roman emperor?
questions.explain: Octavian, Caesar's adopted heir, took the title Augustus in 27 BC. Julius Caesar was dictator but never emperor.
questions.tip: The month August is named for Augustus, the first emperor.

questions.q: What did Roman aqueducts carry?
questions.explain: Aqueducts used gentle slopes to carry water many miles into cities.
questions.tip: Aqua means water: an aqueduct is a water duct.

questions.q: What was the Colosseum mainly used for?
questions.explain: The Colosseum could hold tens of thousands of people watching gladiators and other spectacles.
questions.tip: The Colosseum was colossal: Rome's giant stadium.

questions.q: Which city was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79?
questions.explain: Ash preserved Pompeii so well that archaeologists can see how Romans lived.
questions.tip: Pompeii went poof under ash, frozen in time.

questions.q: Which general crossed the Alps with elephants to attack Rome?
questions.explain: Hannibal of Carthage invaded Italy in 218 BC during the Second Punic War.
questions.tip: Hannibal plus elephants plus Alps: the most surprising road trip ever.

questions.q: In what year is the Western Roman Empire traditionally said to have fallen?
questions.explain: In 476 the Germanic leader Odoacer removed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.
questions.tip: 4-7-6: Rome's western empire ran out of tricks.

questions.q: Which emperor made Byzantium his new capital, later called Constantinople?
questions.explain: Constantine dedicated the city in 330. It is now Istanbul, Turkey.
questions.tip: Constantine's city: Constantinople.

questions.q: What language did the ancient Romans speak?
questions.explain: Latin is the root of Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian, called the Romance languages.
questions.tip: Romance languages come from Rome: Roman-ce!

questions.q: Early Chinese civilization grew along which river, also called the Huang He?
questions.explain: The Yellow River is named for the yellow silt it carries. Its floods could be very deadly.
questions.tip: Huang means yellow: Huang He, the Yellow River.

questions.q: Who was the first emperor to unify China, in 221 BC?
questions.explain: Qin Shi Huang standardized writing, money and measurements. The name China may come from Qin.
questions.tip: Qin (say chin) gave China its name, and its first emperor.

questions.q: What was buried near the first emperor's tomb to guard him?
questions.explain: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers were found by farmers digging a well in 1974.
questions.tip: An army of clay, standing guard all day.

questions.q: Which trade route connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe?
questions.explain: Silk, spices, ideas and religions traveled along the Silk Road.
questions.tip: China's smooth silk slid west on the Silk Road.

questions.q: Which Chinese thinker taught respect for elders, family duty and good government?
questions.explain: Confucius lived about 2,500 years ago. His ideas shaped Chinese society for centuries.
questions.tip: Confucius says: respect your family, and you'll never be confused.

questions.q: During which dynasty was paper invented in China?
questions.explain: Paper was developed during the Han dynasty, about 2,000 years ago.
questions.tip: Hand me some paper: H for Han dynasty.

questions.q: What was the Mandate of Heaven?
choices: The belief that heaven gave rulers the right to rule
questions.explain: If a ruler was cruel or disasters struck, people believed the ruler had lost the Mandate of Heaven.
questions.tip: Rule well or heaven says farewell!

questions.q: What is a dynasty?
choices: A series of rulers from the same family
questions.explain: China was ruled by many dynasties, such as the Shang, Zhou, Qin, Han, Tang, Song, Ming and Qing.
questions.tip: A dynasty is a family business where the business is ruling.

questions.q: Shang dynasty priests wrote questions to their ancestors on what?
questions.explain: Writing carved on bones and shells is the oldest large collection of Chinese writing we know of.
questions.tip: Oracle bones: asking the ancestors and reading the cracks.

questions.q: The Great Wall of China was built mainly to...
choices: Protect against invaders from the north
questions.explain: Walls were built and rebuilt over many dynasties. Much of what stands today is from the Ming dynasty.
questions.tip: The Wall was China's giant fence against northern raiders.

questions.q: In feudalism, what did a lord give a knight in exchange for military service?
questions.explain: Land (called a fief) was exchanged for loyalty and service. Peasants and serfs worked the land.
questions.tip: Feudal and fief both start with F: land for loyalty.

questions.q: Which document did English nobles force King John to accept in 1215?
questions.explain: Magna Carta limited the king's power and said even the king must follow the law.
questions.tip: Magna Carta means great charter: 1215, the king's not supreme.

questions.q: Which disease killed a huge share of Europe's people in the mid-1300s?
questions.explain: The plague spread from 1347 to 1351 and likely killed a third or more of Europe's population.
questions.tip: Fleas on rats carried the plague: tiny biters, giant disaster.

questions.q: Which king was crowned emperor by the Pope on Christmas Day in the year 800?
questions.explain: Charlemagne ruled much of western Europe and encouraged learning.
questions.tip: Charlemagne's Christmas present in 800 was a crown!

questions.q: In 1066, William of Normandy won which battle to conquer England?
questions.explain: William the Conqueror defeated King Harold II, and Norman French rule changed English language and culture.
questions.tip: In ten sixty-six, William won England quick at Hastings.

questions.q: Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg developed which invention in Europe?
choices: A printing press with movable type
questions.explain: Gutenberg's press made books faster and cheaper, spreading ideas across Europe.
questions.tip: Gutenberg made books go from handwritten to printed in a flash.

questions.q: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
questions.explain: The Renaissance began in Italian cities like Florence in the 1300s and 1400s.
questions.tip: Renaissance means rebirth, and it was born in Italy.

questions.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.explain: Michelangelo painted the ceiling from 1508 to 1512. He also carved the statue David.
questions.tip: Michelangelo looked up for four years painting the ceiling: that's a stiff neck!

questions.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explain: Leonardo was a painter, inventor and scientist, a true Renaissance man.
questions.tip: Leonardo drew flying machines and the Mona Lisa smile.

questions.q: In 1517, Martin Luther posted the Ninety-five Theses, starting what movement?
questions.explain: Luther criticized practices of the Catholic Church, especially the sale of indulgences.
questions.tip: 1517: Luther's list reformed the scene.

questions.q: In 1453, which city fell to the Ottoman Turks, ending the Byzantine Empire?
questions.explain: Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, which became the Ottoman capital, later Istanbul.
questions.tip: Istanbul was Constantinople: 1453 was when it changed hands.

questions.q: What was the first plan of government for the United States?
questions.explain: The Articles created a weak national government that could not tax or enforce laws well.
questions.tip: The Articles were the rough draft; the Constitution was the final copy.

questions.q: Which 1786 to 1787 uprising of Massachusetts farmers showed the weakness of the Articles?
questions.explain: Daniel Shays led indebted farmers, and the national government could not easily stop them.
questions.tip: Shays shook the states into writing a stronger plan.

questions.q: Where did the Constitutional Convention meet in 1787?
questions.explain: Delegates met at Independence Hall, the same building where the Declaration was signed.
questions.tip: Philadelphia hosted both: Declaration in '76, Constitution in '87.

questions.q: Who is called the Father of the Constitution?
questions.explain: Madison drafted the Virginia Plan, took detailed notes and later wrote the Bill of Rights.
questions.tip: Madison made the plan: Madison's the Constitution man.

questions.q: The Great Compromise created a Congress with which design?
choices: Senate with equal votes per state, House based on population
One house with equal votes per state
One house based on population only
questions.explain: It blended the Virginia Plan (population) and the New Jersey Plan (equal votes).
questions.tip: Senate = same for every state; House = how many people.

questions.q: What are the first ten amendments to the Constitution called?
questions.explain: The Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791 to protect individual freedoms.
questions.tip: Ten fingers, ten rights: hold up your hands for the Bill of Rights.

questions.q: What are the three branches of the U.S. government?
questions.explain: Congress makes laws, the President carries them out, and the courts interpret them.
questions.tip: Make it, enforce it, judge it: L-E-J.

questions.q: Who wrote the Federalist Papers to support ratifying the Constitution?
questions.explain: The 85 essays were published under the pen name Publius.
questions.tip: H-M-J: Hamilton, Madison, Jay wrote the papers to save the day.

questions.q: Which freedoms does the First Amendment protect?
choices: Religion, speech, press, assembly and petition
questions.explain: The First Amendment protects five freedoms related to belief and expression.
questions.tip: RAPPS: Religion, Assembly, Press, Petition, Speech.

questions.q: What is the system that lets each branch limit the powers of the others called?
questions.explain: For example, the President can veto laws, and Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote.
questions.tip: Like a seesaw, checks and balances keep any one side from going too high.

questions.q: What was Manifest Destiny?
choices: The belief that the U.S. was meant to expand across North America
questions.explain: The phrase, popularized in 1845, was used to justify westward expansion.
questions.tip: Manifest means obvious, destiny means fate: 'obviously fated' to stretch coast to coast.

questions.q: The 1830 Indian Removal Act was signed by which President?
questions.explain: The act led to the forced removal of Native nations from the Southeast to lands west of the Mississippi.
questions.tip: Jackson's act forced nations west against their will.

questions.q: The forced march of the Cherokee to Indian Territory in 1838 to 1839 is called the...
questions.explain: Thousands of Cherokee died from disease, cold and hunger on the journey.
questions.tip: The name tells the sorrow: a trail marked by tears.

questions.q: Which 1836 battle in Texas led to the rallying cry 'Remember the Alamo!'?
questions.explain: Texan defenders were killed at the Alamo. Weeks later, Texans won independence at San Jacinto.
questions.tip: Remember the Alamo, then they won at San Jacinto.

questions.q: Which treaty ended the Mexican-American War in 1848?
questions.explain: Mexico gave up a huge area including California and most of the Southwest.
questions.tip: Guadalupe Hidalgo gave the U.S. a giant Southwest go.

questions.q: Where were the tracks of the first transcontinental railroad joined in 1869?
questions.explain: A golden spike was driven on May 10, 1869, where the Union Pacific and Central Pacific met.
questions.tip: A golden spike in Utah tied East and West together.

questions.q: The Homestead Act of 1862 gave settlers how much land if they farmed it for five years?
questions.explain: Settlers could claim 160 acres of public land by living on and improving it.
questions.tip: 160 acres: a quarter of a square mile, for living on it a while.

questions.q: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 was bought from which country?
questions.explain: Napoleon sold the land for about 15 million dollars.
questions.tip: Napoleon needed cash for wars, so he sold Louisiana: a French yard sale!

questions.q: Who were the forty-niners?
choices: People who rushed to California for gold in 1849
questions.explain: Gold was found in 1848, and about 300,000 people came to California over the next years.
questions.tip: Forty-nine was the year, gold fever was here!

questions.q: Which 1820 agreement admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state?
questions.explain: It also banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of 36 degrees 30 minutes latitude.
questions.tip: Missouri and Maine, two Ms, kept the balance even.

questions.q: In what years was the American Civil War fought?
questions.explain: The war began at Fort Sumter in April 1861 and ended in spring 1865.
questions.tip: Sixty-one to sixty-five: four long years.

questions.q: Where were the first shots of the Civil War fired?
questions.explain: Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor on April 12, 1861.
questions.tip: Sumter started it: S for South Carolina and Start.

questions.q: Who was President of the Confederacy?
questions.explain: Jefferson Davis led the Confederate government, while Robert E. Lee led its main army.
questions.tip: Davis led the South's government, Lee led the South's army.

questions.q: Which general led the Union armies to victory and later became President?
questions.explain: Grant became the Union's top general in 1864 and was elected President in 1868.
questions.tip: Grant was granted the win, then the White House.

questions.q: Which 1863 battle in Pennsylvania is considered a major turning point of the war?
questions.explain: Lee's invasion of the North was stopped at Gettysburg, July 1 to 3, 1863.
questions.tip: At Gettysburg the South didn't get the win.

questions.q: How does Lincoln's Gettysburg Address begin?
choices: Four score and seven years ago
When in the course of human events
questions.explain: A score is 20, so four score and seven is 87 years: back to 1776.

questions.q: Where did Robert E. Lee surrender to Ulysses S. Grant in April 1865?
questions.explain: Lee surrendered on April 9, 1865, effectively ending the war.
questions.tip: Appomattox: the war was put back in its box.

questions.q: Who assassinated Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in April 1865?
questions.explain: Booth, a Confederate sympathizer, shot Lincoln on April 14, 1865. Lincoln died the next morning.
questions.tip: Booth struck in a theater box: a tragedy on a stage.

questions.q: Which amendment abolished slavery in the United States?
questions.explain: The 13th Amendment was ratified in December 1865.
questions.tip: 13, 14, 15: freedom, citizenship, vote, the Reconstruction team.

questions.q: Which novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe turned many Northerners against slavery?
questions.explain: Published in 1852, it became a bestseller and stirred anti-slavery feelings.
questions.tip: Stowe's book about a cabin shook the whole nation.

questions.q: The rebuilding of the South after the Civil War is called...
questions.explain: Reconstruction lasted from 1865 to 1877.
questions.tip: Re-construct means build again.

questions.q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin in the late 1700s?
questions.explain: Britain had coal, iron, capital, colonies for markets and a growing workforce.
questions.tip: Britain had the coal to get the whole thing rolling.

questions.q: Which inventor greatly improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s?
questions.explain: Watt's separate condenser made steam engines far more efficient. The unit of power, the watt, is named for him.
questions.tip: What powered the revolution? Watt's steam engine!

questions.q: Which industry was the first to be transformed by factories and machines?
questions.explain: Inventions like the spinning jenny and water frame moved spinning and weaving into factories.
questions.tip: The revolution started with thread: spin it, weave it, factory-made.

questions.q: Eli Whitney's cotton gin of 1793 had which major effect?
choices: It made cotton profitable and expanded slavery in the South
questions.explain: The gin quickly separated seeds from cotton, so planters grew far more cotton and relied even more on enslaved labor.
questions.tip: Gin is short for engine; it sped up cotton but deepened slavery.

questions.q: Andrew Carnegie made his fortune mainly in which industry?
questions.explain: Carnegie Steel became U.S. Steel in 1901. Carnegie later gave much of his fortune to libraries and education.
questions.tip: Carnegie = steel, Rockefeller = oil: C-S and R-O.

questions.q: John D. Rockefeller controlled most of the U.S. oil refining business through which company?
questions.explain: Standard Oil was broken up by the Supreme Court in 1911 for violating antitrust law.
questions.tip: Rockefeller set the standard in oil.

questions.q: Which 1890 law was the first federal law against monopolies?
questions.explain: The Sherman Act banned contracts and combinations that restrained trade.
questions.tip: Sherman marched against the trusts: first law to bust.

questions.q: The 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York led to...
choices: The end of child labor worldwide
The invention of the fire truck
questions.explain: 146 workers, mostly young immigrant women, died partly because exits were locked. New York passed many safety reforms.
questions.tip: Locked doors, lost lives, new laws.

questions.q: Upton Sinclair's 1906 novel The Jungle exposed conditions in which industry?
questions.explain: The book led to the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act in 1906.
questions.tip: Sinclair said he aimed for the public's heart but hit its stomach.

questions.q: Who introduced the moving assembly line for making cars in 1913?
questions.explain: The assembly line cut the time to build a Model T from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes.
questions.tip: Ford made cars move down the line so they could move down the road.

questions.q: Writers who exposed corruption and social problems in the early 1900s were called...
questions.explain: Theodore Roosevelt coined the term, comparing them to someone raking up muck.
questions.tip: Muckrakers raked up the muck so the public could see it.

questions.q: In what years was World War I fought?
questions.explain: The war began in summer 1914 and ended with an armistice in November 1918.
questions.tip: WWI: 14 to 18, four years in between.

questions.q: Whose assassination in Sarajevo in June 1914 triggered World War I?
questions.explain: Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb, shot the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne.
questions.tip: Franz Ferdinand's death was the spark that lit the powder keg of Europe.

questions.q: Historians often summarize the long-term causes of WWI with which acronym?
questions.explain: MAIN stands for Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism and Nationalism.
questions.tip: The MAIN causes: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism.

questions.q: Which of these was one of the Central Powers in World War I?
questions.explain: The Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria.
questions.tip: Central Powers sat in the center of Europe: Germany and Austria-Hungary.

questions.q: What 1917 message from Germany proposing an alliance with Mexico helped push the U.S. into the war?
questions.explain: Britain decoded it, and it promised Mexico lost U.S. territory if it joined Germany.
questions.tip: Zimmermann's zinger told Mexico to zap the U.S.: big mistake.

questions.q: The sinking of which British passenger ship in 1915 killed 128 Americans and angered the U.S.?
questions.explain: A German U-boat sank the Lusitania on May 7, 1915.
questions.tip: Lusitania was lost to a U-boat; Titanic was lost to an iceberg.

questions.q: In what month and year did the United States enter World War I?
questions.explain: Congress declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917.
questions.tip: The U.S. joined late, in '17, when the war was almost three years in.

questions.q: What type of fighting, with soldiers in long dug-in lines, defined the Western Front?
questions.explain: Trenches stretched from the North Sea to Switzerland, and attacks across no man's land were deadly.
questions.tip: WWI soldiers dug in and stayed in: trench life.

questions.q: The armistice ending WWI fighting took effect at 11 a.m. on which date?
questions.explain: It was the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month. Veterans Day is held on that date.
questions.tip: 11-11-11: hour, day and month all elevens.

questions.q: Which treaty, signed in 1919, made Germany accept blame for the war and pay reparations?
questions.explain: Its war guilt clause and heavy terms caused deep resentment in Germany.
questions.tip: Versailles was the palace where Germany paid the price.

questions.q: Woodrow Wilson's plan for peace, including a League of Nations, was called the...
questions.explain: The U.S. Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, so the U.S. never joined the League.
questions.tip: Wilson had 14 points, but the Senate made the League pointless for the U.S.

g912.name: The Great Depression and World War II

questions.q: The Great Depression began with a stock market crash in which year?
questions.explain: Stocks collapsed in October 1929, including Black Tuesday on October 29.
questions.tip: 1929: the market fell down the line.

questions.q: Franklin D. Roosevelt's programs to fight the Depression were called the...
questions.explain: The New Deal created jobs programs, banking reforms and Social Security.
questions.tip: FDR dealt the nation a new hand of cards: the New Deal.

questions.q: What event on September 1, 1939, started World War II in Europe?
questions.explain: Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later.
questions.tip: Poland first in '39: Hitler crossed the line.

questions.q: On what date did Japan attack Pearl Harbor?
questions.explain: FDR called it a date which will live in infamy. The U.S. declared war on Japan the next day.
questions.tip: December 7th, '41: a date which will live in infamy.

questions.q: Which three main countries made up the Axis Powers?
questions.explain: Germany, Italy and Japan signed the Tripartite Pact in 1940.
questions.tip: GIJ: Germany, Italy, Japan, the Axis gang.

questions.q: D-Day, the Allied invasion of Normandy, France, took place on which date?
questions.explain: It was the largest seaborne invasion in history, opening a western front against Germany.
questions.tip: D-Day in June, 6-6-44: Allies landed on the shore.

questions.q: About how many Jewish people were murdered in the Holocaust?
questions.explain: Nazi Germany systematically murdered about six million Jews, along with millions of others.
questions.tip: Six million: a number we must never forget.

questions.q: Which 1942 naval battle is considered the turning point of the war in the Pacific?
questions.explain: The U.S. sank four Japanese aircraft carriers at Midway in June 1942.
questions.tip: Midway was midway through the Pacific war, where the tide turned.

questions.q: Which battle in the Soviet Union, ending in early 1943, was a major turning point on the Eastern Front?
questions.explain: A whole German army was surrounded and surrendered at Stalingrad in February 1943.
questions.tip: At Stalingrad, Germany's advance stalled.

questions.q: On which two Japanese cities did the U.S. drop atomic bombs in August 1945?
questions.explain: Hiroshima was bombed on August 6 and Nagasaki on August 9. Japan announced its surrender days later.
questions.tip: H before N, like in the alphabet: Hiroshima, then Nagasaki.

questions.q: Executive Order 9066 in 1942 led to what?
choices: Forced removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans
questions.explain: About 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them U.S. citizens, were sent to camps. The U.S. formally apologized in 1988.
questions.tip: 9066 took homes away; in 1988 the nation said sorry.

questions.q: Which international organization was founded in 1945 to keep world peace?
questions.explain: The UN replaced the failed League of Nations. Its headquarters is in New York City.
questions.tip: After WWII, the nations united: the UN.

questions.q: The Cold War was a rivalry mainly between which two countries?
choices: The United States and the Soviet Union
questions.explain: It lasted from about 1947 to 1991 and was fought through arms races, proxy wars and propaganda.
questions.tip: Cold because the two superpowers never fought each other directly.

questions.q: The U.S. policy of stopping the spread of communism was called...
questions.explain: The Truman Doctrine of 1947 put containment into action by aiding Greece and Turkey.
questions.tip: Contain it like a lid on a jar.

questions.q: Which U.S. program gave billions of dollars to rebuild Western Europe after WWII?
questions.explain: Named for Secretary of State George Marshall, it helped European economies recover and resist communism.
questions.tip: Marshall marshaled money to rebuild Europe.

questions.q: In 1948 to 1949, the U.S. and Britain flew supplies to which blockaded city?
questions.explain: The Berlin Airlift delivered food and fuel until the Soviets lifted the blockade.
questions.tip: Berlin got groceries by airplane!

questions.q: Which military alliance did the U.S. and Western European nations form in 1949?
questions.explain: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization promised that an attack on one is an attack on all.
questions.tip: NATO: North Atlantic friends, all for one and one for all.

questions.q: The Korean War ended in 1953 with what result?
choices: A U.S. defeat and retreat from Asia
A peace treaty signed by all sides
questions.explain: No peace treaty was signed, and Korea remains divided at about the same line.
questions.tip: Korea: started at the 38th, ended at the 38th.

questions.q: What did the Soviet Union launch in 1957, starting the Space Race?
choices: The first person on the Moon
questions.explain: Sputnik's launch alarmed Americans and led to NASA's creation in 1958.
questions.tip: Sputnik went beep-beep, and the U.S. went 'eep!'

questions.q: In October 1962, the U.S. and USSR came close to nuclear war over missiles in which country?
questions.explain: President Kennedy ordered a naval quarantine, and Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles.
questions.tip: Thirteen tense days in October '62, with missiles in Cuba.

questions.q: When did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.explain: East Germany opened the border crossings, and people began tearing down the wall.
questions.tip: Up in '61, down in '89: the wall stood for 28 years.

questions.q: In what year did the Soviet Union dissolve?
questions.explain: Gorbachev resigned on December 25, 1991, and the USSR split into 15 countries.
questions.tip: The wall fell in '89, the whole union two years down the line.

questions.q: The fall of Saigon in 1975 marked the end of which war?
questions.explain: North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon on April 30, 1975, and Vietnam was unified under communist rule.
questions.tip: Saigon fell in '75, and it's now called Ho Chi Minh City.

questions.q: Which 1954 Supreme Court case ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional?
questions.explain: The Court unanimously ruled that separate schools are inherently unequal.
questions.tip: Brown beat Plessy: separate is not equal.

questions.q: Which 1896 case had allowed 'separate but equal' segregation?
questions.explain: Plessy v. Ferguson upheld segregation on railroad cars, and the idea spread widely until Brown overturned it in schools.
questions.tip: Plessy: separate, but not really equal.

questions.q: Rosa Parks's arrest in 1955 sparked which protest?
questions.explain: Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, refused to ride city buses for 381 days.
questions.tip: 381 days of walking until the buses were fair.

questions.q: In 1957, President Eisenhower sent federal troops to protect nine Black students at a high school in which city?
questions.explain: The Little Rock Nine integrated Central High School under the protection of the 101st Airborne.
questions.tip: Nine students stood strong as a rock in Little Rock.

questions.q: In 1960, Black college students in Greensboro, North Carolina, began which kind of protest?
choices: Sit-ins at a segregated lunch counter
questions.explain: Four students sat at a Woolworth's counter and asked to be served, and sit-ins spread across the South.
questions.tip: They sat down to stand up for their rights.

questions.q: At which 1963 event did Martin Luther King Jr. give his 'I Have a Dream' speech?
questions.explain: About 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial on August 28, 1963.
questions.tip: Dream at the Lincoln Memorial: Lincoln and King together on the steps.

questions.q: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 do?
choices: Banned discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin
Gave women the right to vote
Ended the poll tax in state elections
questions.explain: Signed by Lyndon B. Johnson, it outlawed segregation in public places and discrimination in employment.
questions.tip: 1964: no more 'whites only' on the door.

questions.q: The 1965 marches from Selma to Montgomery led to which law?
questions.explain: Violence against marchers on Bloody Sunday shocked the nation, and Congress passed the Voting Rights Act.
questions.tip: Selma for the vote: march for the ballot.

questions.q: What did the 24th Amendment, ratified in 1964, ban?
questions.explain: Poll taxes had been used to keep poor and Black citizens from voting.
questions.tip: 24th: no paying to vote.

questions.q: Riders who challenged segregated interstate buses in 1961 were called...
questions.explain: Black and white activists rode buses together into the South and faced violent attacks.
questions.tip: Freedom Riders rode for the right to ride.

questions.q: Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in 1968 in which city?
questions.explain: King was in Memphis to support striking sanitation workers when he was killed on April 4, 1968.
questions.tip: Memphis, April '68: King was there for workers' rights.

questions.q: The Spanish-American War of 1898 gave the U.S. control of which territories?
choices: Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines
questions.explain: The war followed the explosion of the USS Maine in Havana harbor. Cuba became independent under U.S. influence.
questions.tip: Remember the Maine and the three new islands: P-G-P.

questions.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1920, gave women the right to vote?
questions.explain: The 19th Amendment barred denying the vote on account of sex.
questions.tip: 19 for the women of 1920.

questions.q: Prohibition of alcohol was created by the 18th Amendment and ended by which amendment?
questions.explain: The 21st Amendment, ratified in 1933, repealed Prohibition. It is the only amendment that repeals another.
questions.tip: 21 is the drinking age, and the 21st brought drinks back.

questions.q: The 16th Amendment of 1913 allowed Congress to create what?
questions.explain: The 17th Amendment, also from 1913, created direct election of senators.
questions.tip: Sweet 16 brought the not-so-sweet income tax.

questions.q: Which President was nicknamed the 'trust buster'?
questions.explain: Theodore Roosevelt used the Sherman Antitrust Act against big monopolies.
questions.tip: Teddy busted trusts with his big stick.

questions.q: The 1920s flowering of Black art, music and literature centered in New York is called the...
questions.explain: Writers like Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston and musicians like Duke Ellington were part of it.
questions.tip: Harlem's rebirth of art: Renaissance means rebirth.

questions.q: Severe drought and dust storms on the Great Plains in the 1930s are known as the...
questions.explain: Poor farming practices and drought turned topsoil to dust. Many families moved west to California.
questions.tip: The Plains turned into a giant bowl of dust.

questions.q: Which President was elected four times, leading to the 22nd Amendment's two-term limit?
questions.explain: FDR won in 1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944. The 22nd Amendment was ratified in 1951.
questions.tip: FDR: Four-time Democratic Roosevelt.

questions.q: The Social Security Act was passed in which year as part of the New Deal?
questions.explain: It created old-age pensions and unemployment insurance.
questions.tip: Social Security '35: helping seniors stay alive and thrive.

questions.q: Which President resigned in 1974 because of the Watergate scandal?
questions.explain: Nixon is the only U.S. President to resign. Gerald Ford took over.
questions.tip: Watergate washed Nixon out in '74.

questions.q: Which canal, opened in 1914, connected the Atlantic and Pacific oceans?
questions.explain: Built by the U.S., it saved ships the long trip around South America.
questions.tip: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama! (It reads the same backward.)

questions.q: The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789, began which revolution?
questions.explain: Parisians stormed the royal fortress and prison. July 14 is France's national holiday.
questions.tip: Bastille Day is France's Fourth of July.

questions.q: Napoleon was finally defeated at which battle in 1815?
questions.explain: British and Prussian armies beat Napoleon in present-day Belgium, and he was exiled to Saint Helena.
questions.tip: To 'meet your Waterloo' means a final defeat, just like Napoleon.

questions.q: Who led the Bolsheviks to power in Russia in 1917?
questions.explain: The Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917 and later formed the Soviet Union.
questions.tip: Lenin led first; Stalin came later.

questions.q: Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in which year?
questions.explain: Mao's communists won the civil war, and the Nationalists retreated to Taiwan.
questions.tip: 1949: China's communist new line.

questions.q: Who led India's nonviolent independence movement against British rule?
questions.explain: India gained independence on August 15, 1947, and was partitioned into India and Pakistan.
questions.tip: Gandhi's Salt March: freedom one step at a time.

questions.q: Nelson Mandela became South Africa's first Black president in which year, after the end of apartheid?
questions.explain: Mandela spent 27 years in prison before being freed in 1990 and elected in 1994.
questions.tip: 27 years in prison, then president in '94.

questions.q: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to rapid modernization in which country?
questions.explain: Japan adopted Western technology, industry and a modern army within a few decades.
questions.tip: Meiji means enlightened rule: Japan switched on the lights of industry.

questions.q: The 1884 to 1885 Berlin Conference set rules for European powers to divide which continent?
questions.explain: It sped up the Scramble for Africa. By 1914, nearly all of Africa was under European control.
questions.tip: Berlin set the rules, then the Scramble for Africa took off.

questions.q: Which country became the first independent Black republic after a revolution of enslaved people in 1804?
questions.explain: The Haitian Revolution, led at first by Toussaint Louverture, defeated French forces.
questions.tip: Haiti: the only nation born from a successful revolt of enslaved people.

questions.q: Simon Bolivar is famous for leading independence movements in which region?
questions.explain: Bolivar helped free Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain. Bolivia is named for him.
questions.tip: Bolivia is named for Bolivar, El Libertador.

questions.q: The State of Israel declared independence in which year?
questions.explain: Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, and war with neighboring Arab states followed.
questions.tip: 1948: Israel's founding date.

questions.q: What is historiography?
choices: The study of how history has been written and interpreted
The study of ancient handwriting only
questions.explain: Historiography examines historians' methods, sources and interpretations, and how they change over time.
questions.tip: History is the past; historiography is the history of writing about the past.

questions.q: Which is a primary source for studying the American Revolution?
choices: A letter written by a Continental soldier in 1777
A textbook chapter on the Revolution
questions.explain: Primary sources were created at the time by participants or witnesses; secondary sources analyze them later.
questions.tip: Primary = present at the time; secondary = studied it later.

questions.q: Which Greek writer is often called the 'Father of History'?
questions.explain: Cicero gave Herodotus this title. His Histories describe the Greco-Persian Wars.
questions.tip: Herodotus: HEro of HIStory, the first to inquire.

questions.q: Which ancient historian wrote a careful, evidence-focused account of the Peloponnesian War?
questions.explain: Thucydides, an Athenian general, emphasized causes, power politics and eyewitness evidence.
questions.tip: Thucydides was tough on sources: the hard-nosed historian.

questions.q: The French Annales school of history emphasized what?
choices: Long-term social, economic and geographic structures
The deeds of great kings only
questions.explain: Founded by Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre in 1929, it later produced Fernand Braudel's idea of the longue duree.
questions.tip: Annales looks at the long haul, not just the latest headline.

questions.q: The term 'Whig history' criticizes which approach?
choices: Telling the past as inevitable progress toward the present
Writing only about Britain's Whig party
questions.explain: Herbert Butterfield named and criticized it in The Whig Interpretation of History (1931).
questions.tip: Whig history wears present-day glasses and sees an arrow pointing straight at us.

questions.q: Which 19th-century German historian championed archival research to show the past 'as it actually was'?
questions.explain: Ranke helped found modern professional, source-based history.
questions.tip: Ranke ranked archives first.
