questions.q: E. P. Thompson's The Making of the English Working Class (1963) is a classic of which approach?
questions.explain: Thompson sought to rescue ordinary workers from what he called 'the enormous condescension of posterity'.
questions.tip: History from below: start at the bottom, not the throne.

questions.q: What is 'presentism' in historical writing?
choices: Judging or interpreting the past by today's values and assumptions
questions.explain: Historians try to understand people in their own context, even while asking questions shaped by the present.
questions.tip: Presentism puts the past in a present-day costume.

questions.q: Frederick Jackson Turner's 1893 'frontier thesis' argued what?
choices: The frontier shaped American democracy and character
The frontier had no effect on America
America was shaped mainly by its cities
questions.explain: Turner argued that the frontier experience fostered individualism and democracy; later historians challenged it.
questions.tip: Turner turned to the frontier to explain America.

questions.q: Edward Said's 1978 book Orientalism critiqued what?
choices: Western representations of the Middle East and Asia
questions.explain: Said argued that Western scholarship built a stereotyped 'Orient' tied to imperial power.
questions.tip: Said said the West's picture of the East said more about the West.

questions.q: Which 14th-century North African scholar wrote the Muqaddimah, a pioneering theory of history and society?
questions.explain: Ibn Khaldun analyzed the rise and fall of dynasties through group solidarity, called asabiyyah.
questions.tip: Ibn Khaldun wrote history's 'introduction': Muqaddimah means introduction.

questions.q: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended which war?
questions.explain: It is often cited as a foundation of the modern system of sovereign states.
questions.tip: Westphalia: 30 years of war, then states were sovereign for sure.

questions.q: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly found lands outside Europe between which two powers?
questions.explain: The line explains why Brazil speaks Portuguese while most of Latin America speaks Spanish.
questions.tip: Brazil bulged east of the line, so Portugal got it.

questions.q: Which treaty ended the Seven Years' War (French and Indian War) in 1763?
questions.explain: France gave up Canada and lands east of the Mississippi to Britain. Britain's war debt led to new colonial taxes.
questions.tip: Paris 1763 ended one war and planted the seeds of the next one in 1775.

questions.q: Which treaty formally recognized American independence?
questions.explain: Britain recognized the United States and its borders east of the Mississippi.
questions.tip: Two Paris treaties, twenty years apart: 1763 and 1783.

questions.q: The Congress of Vienna (1814 to 1815) aimed to do what?
choices: Restore a balance of power in Europe after Napoleon
questions.explain: Led by figures like Austria's Metternich, it redrew borders and restored monarchies.
questions.tip: Vienna put Europe back together after Napoleon broke it.

questions.q: The Treaty of Nanking (1842) ended the First Opium War and gave Britain which territory?
questions.explain: It also opened treaty ports and began what China calls the 'century of humiliation'.
questions.tip: Nanking handed over Hong Kong.

questions.q: Which 1918 treaty took Russia out of World War I?
questions.explain: The Bolsheviks gave up huge territories to the Central Powers to exit the war.
questions.tip: Brest-Litovsk: Lenin left the war and lost land.

questions.q: The 1916 Sykes-Picot Agreement secretly divided which region into British and French spheres?
questions.explain: It shaped postwar borders in areas such as Syria, Iraq and Lebanon.
questions.tip: Sykes (British) and Picot (French) drew lines in the sand.

questions.q: The 1957 Treaty of Rome created what?
questions.explain: The EEC built a common market among six founding states and was a forerunner of the European Union.
questions.tip: All roads lead to Rome, and the road to the EU started there.

questions.q: Which 1992 treaty established the European Union?
questions.explain: Maastricht created the EU and laid out the path to a common currency, the euro.
questions.tip: Maastricht made the EU and the euro match.

questions.q: The Treaty of Utrecht (1713) ended which war?
choices: The War of the Spanish Succession
questions.explain: It confirmed a Bourbon on Spain's throne but barred union with France; Britain gained Gibraltar.
questions.tip: Utrecht settled who sat on Spain's throne, and Britain got the Rock of Gibraltar.

questions.q: England's Glorious Revolution of 1688 placed which monarchs on the throne?
questions.explain: James II was replaced, and the 1689 English Bill of Rights limited royal power.
questions.tip: Glorious because it was mostly bloodless in England: William and Mary, no scary.

questions.q: In June 1789, members of France's Third Estate swore not to disband until France had a constitution. What is this called?
questions.explain: Locked out of their meeting hall, they gathered in a nearby indoor tennis court.
questions.tip: Locked out, they took the oath on a tennis court: game, set, revolution.

questions.q: Who was the leading figure of the Reign of Terror during the French Revolution?
questions.explain: Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety ordered thousands of executions before he was guillotined in 1794.
questions.tip: Robespierre's Terror ended with his own trip to the guillotine.

questions.q: Which 1789 French document proclaimed natural rights such as liberty and equality before the law?
choices: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
questions.explain: It was influenced by Enlightenment ideas and the American Declaration of Independence.
questions.tip: Liberty, equality, fraternity: rights for man and citizen.

questions.q: The wave of uprisings across Europe in 1848 is often called the...
questions.explain: Revolts in France, the German states, the Austrian Empire and Italy demanded liberal reforms and national unity; most were suppressed.
questions.tip: 1848: a revolutionary spring that froze over by winter.

questions.q: Which 1911 revolution ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule in China?
questions.explain: The Qing dynasty fell, and the last emperor, Puyi, abdicated in 1912. Sun Yat-sen was a key leader.
questions.tip: 1911: the dynasty system fell, and the Republic of China began.

questions.q: In Russia, which government ruled between the February and October revolutions of 1917?
questions.explain: Alexander Kerensky became its leader; the Bolsheviks overthrew it in October.
questions.tip: Provisional means temporary, and it was: February to October.

questions.q: The Mexican Revolution began in 1910 against the long rule of which president?
questions.explain: Diaz had ruled for over three decades. Leaders like Madero, Zapata and Villa fought in the revolution.
questions.tip: Diaz's days were done in 1910.

questions.q: The 1979 revolution in Iran brought which leader to power?
questions.explain: The Shah was overthrown, and Iran became an Islamic Republic.
questions.tip: 1979: the Shah went out, the Ayatollah came in.

questions.q: Crane Brinton's The Anatomy of Revolution compared revolutions to what?
questions.explain: Brinton described a pattern of early symptoms, a crisis stage (often a radical terror) and recovery.
questions.tip: Revolution as fever: symptoms, crisis, then the fever breaks.

questions.q: Copernicus's 1543 book, a starting point of the Scientific Revolution, argued what?
questions.explain: His heliocentric model was later supported by Galileo and Kepler and explained by Newton.
questions.tip: Helio means sun: Copernicus put the Sun in the center.

questions.q: Which empire, founded by Genghis Khan, became the largest contiguous land empire in history?
questions.explain: At its peak in the 1200s, it stretched from Korea to Eastern Europe.
questions.tip: Mongols on horseback rode the biggest land empire ever.

questions.q: Which Ottoman sultan conquered Constantinople in 1453?
questions.explain: Mehmed II, called the Conqueror, made the city his capital.
questions.tip: Mehmed the Conqueror conquered Constantinople: two Cs.

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife?
questions.explain: Shah Jahan built it in Agra for Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631.
questions.tip: Shah Jahan, Taj Mahal: a palace of love made of marble.

questions.q: What was the capital of the Aztec Empire?
questions.explain: Tenochtitlan was built on an island in Lake Texcoco; Mexico City stands on its site.
questions.tip: Aztecs built on a lake; the Inca built in the Andes at Cusco.

questions.q: Mansa Musa, famous for his enormous wealth and his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, ruled which empire?
questions.explain: He reportedly spent so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell.
questions.tip: Mansa Musa made it rain gold in Mali.

questions.q: The Byzantine emperor Justinian is known for what legal achievement?
questions.explain: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis, in the 500s, became a foundation of civil law in Europe.
questions.tip: Justinian made Roman law just-in-one-place.

questions.q: The House of Wisdom, a famous center of learning, was located in which Abbasid capital?
questions.explain: Scholars there translated Greek and Persian works and advanced mathematics and astronomy.
questions.tip: Baghdad's House of Wisdom: a library that lit up the golden age.

questions.q: Which philosopher joked that the Holy Roman Empire was 'neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire'?
questions.explain: The Holy Roman Empire was finally dissolved in 1806 during the Napoleonic Wars.
questions.tip: Voltaire's triple 'neither' is the best roast in history.

questions.q: Which ruler founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire?
questions.explain: Cyrus conquered Media, Lydia and Babylon in the 500s BC and was known for tolerating local customs.
questions.tip: Cyrus started it, Darius organized it, and Alexander finished it off.

questions.q: What was the last imperial dynasty of China?
questions.explain: The Qing, founded by the Manchus, ruled from 1644 until 1912.
questions.tip: Qing was the final king (well, emperor) of China.

questions.q: The Inca built a vast road network and kept records using knotted cords called...
questions.explain: Quipu used knots and colors to record numbers and possibly other information.
questions.tip: Quipu: keeping count with knots.

questions.q: In 1947, British India was partitioned into which two independent states?
questions.explain: Partition caused mass migration and violence. East Pakistan later became Bangladesh in 1971.
questions.tip: 1947: one empire split in two, and in 1971 Bangladesh split from Pakistan.

questions.q: Kwame Nkrumah led which country to independence from Britain in 1957?
questions.explain: The Gold Coast became Ghana, inspiring independence movements across Africa.
questions.tip: The Gold Coast went green, gold and red as Ghana.

questions.q: Algeria won independence from France in 1962 after a war that began in which year?
questions.explain: The Algerian War was long and brutal and also brought down France's Fourth Republic in 1958.
questions.tip: Eight years of war, '54 to '62.

questions.q: The 1955 Bandung Conference in Indonesia brought together nations from which regions?
questions.explain: Newly independent states promoted cooperation and opposed colonialism, foreshadowing the Non-Aligned Movement.
questions.tip: Bandung banded Asia and Africa together.

questions.q: In the 1956 Suez Crisis, which Egyptian leader nationalized the Suez Canal?
questions.explain: Britain, France and Israel invaded, but U.S. and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw.
questions.tip: Nasser took the canal, and Britain learned its empire days were over.

questions.q: Which 1954 battle ended French colonial rule in Indochina?
questions.explain: Viet Minh forces defeated the French, and the Geneva Accords divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel.
questions.tip: Dien Bien Phu: France's final 'phew' in Vietnam.

questions.q: 1960 is often called the 'Year of Africa' because...
questions.explain: Many former French colonies, plus Nigeria, Somalia and the Congo, became independent that year.
questions.tip: 1960: 17 new flags flew in one year.

questions.q: Who was the first prime minister of the independent Congo in 1960?
questions.explain: Lumumba was overthrown and killed in 1961 amid the Congo Crisis.
questions.tip: Lumumba led first, but only briefly.

questions.q: Which thinker wrote The Wretched of the Earth (1961), an influential work on colonialism?
questions.explain: Fanon, a psychiatrist from Martinique, analyzed the psychological and political effects of colonial rule.
questions.tip: Fanon fanned the flames of anti-colonial thought.

questions.q: Jomo Kenyatta became the first leader of which independent nation in 1963?
questions.explain: Kenya's path to independence included the Mau Mau uprising against British rule.
questions.tip: Kenyatta led Kenya: the names almost match.

questions.q: Indonesia declared independence in 1945 from which colonial power?
questions.explain: Sukarno declared independence; the Dutch recognized it in 1949 after years of conflict.
questions.tip: The Dutch East Indies became Indonesia.

questions.q: What is the Columbian Exchange?
choices: The transfer of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492
A treaty between Spain and Portugal
questions.explain: Potatoes and maize went east; horses, wheat and devastating diseases like smallpox came west.
questions.tip: Potatoes went to Ireland, horses came to the Plains: the great swap after Columbus.

questions.q: Which disease from Europe was the deadliest for Native American populations?
questions.explain: Indigenous peoples had no immunity, and epidemics killed a large majority in many regions.
questions.tip: Small name, enormous toll: smallpox.

questions.q: How did the Black Death change European society in the long run?
choices: Labor shortages raised wages and weakened serfdom
questions.explain: With fewer workers, surviving peasants could demand more, and landlords lost power.
questions.tip: Fewer hands meant workers could demand a bigger slice.

questions.q: How did the printing press help the Protestant Reformation spread?
choices: Luther's ideas were printed and distributed quickly and widely
It let the Pope ban all books
questions.explain: Pamphlets and Bibles in local languages spread faster than authorities could suppress them.
questions.tip: Luther went viral, 1500s style.

questions.q: How did the Seven Years' War help cause the American Revolution?
choices: Britain's war debt led to new taxes on the colonies
It ended all trade with Britain
questions.explain: Acts like the Stamp Act aimed to raise colonial revenue, sparking protests.
questions.tip: Britain won the war but sent the bill to the colonies.

questions.q: Historians distinguish the immediate cause of WWI (Franz Ferdinand's assassination) from what?
choices: Underlying long-term causes like alliances and nationalism
questions.explain: A spark (proximate cause) needs fuel (underlying causes) to start a fire.
questions.tip: Spark vs. fuel: the assassination lit a pile that was already stacked.

questions.q: Which consequence of the Great Depression helped extremist parties rise in 1930s Europe?
questions.explain: In Germany, unemployment soared and the Nazi vote surged in the early 1930s.
questions.tip: Empty wallets opened doors for extremists.

questions.q: What is a counterfactual question in history?
choices: Asking what might have happened if one event had gone differently
questions.explain: Counterfactuals can help weigh which causes mattered most, though they cannot be proven.
questions.tip: Counterfactual = 'What if...?'

questions.q: A major consequence of World War II for European colonial empires was...
questions.explain: Exhausted European powers faced strong independence movements and pressure from the U.S. and USSR.
questions.tip: The war broke Europe's grip, and colonies slipped free.

questions.q: Which factor is commonly cited as a cause of the decline of the Western Roman Empire?
choices: Political instability and pressure from migrating peoples
questions.explain: Historians point to many factors: civil wars, economic strain, overextension and Germanic migrations.
questions.tip: Rome wasn't built in a day, and it didn't fall in one either.

questions.q: Which came first: the Declaration of Independence or the signing of the U.S. Constitution?
questions.explain: The Declaration came 11 years before the Constitution; the Articles of Confederation governed in between.
questions.tip: First you declare you're leaving, then you write the house rules.

questions.q: Which came first: the Louisiana Purchase or the Lewis and Clark expedition?
questions.explain: Jefferson bought the land, then sent Lewis and Clark to explore it.
questions.tip: Buy the house, then tour it.

questions.q: Which happened first: the War of 1812 or the Mexican-American War?
questions.explain: The War of 1812 was fought against Britain, decades before the war with Mexico.
questions.tip: The year is right in the name: 1812 beats 1846.

questions.q: Which came first: the end of the Civil War or the completion of the transcontinental railroad?
questions.explain: The railroad was finished in 1869, four years after the war ended.
questions.tip: Peace first, then the golden spike.

questions.q: Which came first: women's suffrage (19th Amendment) or the 1929 stock market crash?
questions.explain: Women gained the vote nationally in 1920, at the start of the Roaring Twenties.
questions.tip: The Twenties started with ballots and ended with a crash.

questions.q: Which came first: the Korean War or the Vietnam War's major U.S. troop buildup?
questions.explain: Korea was the first major Cold War 'hot' war; large U.S. combat deployments to Vietnam began in 1965.
questions.tip: K before V, in the alphabet and in history.

questions.q: Which came first: Sputnik or the Moon landing?
questions.explain: Sputnik started the Space Race; Apollo 11 landed on the Moon 12 years later.
questions.tip: First the beep, then the giant leap.

questions.q: Which came first: the fall of the Berlin Wall or the breakup of the Soviet Union?
questions.explain: Revolutions in Eastern Europe in 1989 preceded the USSR's collapse two years later.
questions.tip: The wall cracked first, then the whole house fell.

questions.q: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
questions.explain: The Great Pyramid dates to about 2560 BC; Cleopatra died in 30 BC, about 2,000 years before 1969.
questions.tip: Ancient Egypt was ancient even to Cleopatra.

questions.q: Which came first: Magna Carta or Columbus's first voyage?
questions.explain: Magna Carta was sealed almost 300 years before Columbus sailed.
questions.tip: 1215 has a 2 in the hundreds; 1492 has a 4: Magna Carta wins.

questions.q: Which came first: Pearl Harbor or the start of World War II in Europe?
questions.explain: Germany invaded Poland in September 1939; the U.S. entered the war after Pearl Harbor in December 1941.
questions.tip: Europe had been fighting two years before America joined.

questions.q: Which came first: Brown v. Board of Education or the Montgomery Bus Boycott?
questions.explain: Brown came in May 1954; the boycott began in December 1955.
questions.tip: Schools first, then buses.

questions.q: When was the American Revolutionary War fought?
questions.explain: It began at Lexington and Concord in 1775 and ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
questions.tip: 75 to 83: the war began before the Declaration and outlasted Yorktown.

questions.q: The War of 1812 was fought between the United States and which country?
questions.explain: Issues included impressment of American sailors and trade restrictions. The British burned Washington in 1814.
questions.tip: Round two against Britain: the White House burned, and the anthem was born.

questions.q: The Battle of New Orleans (January 1815) was fought after which event?
choices: The Treaty of Ghent had already been signed
questions.explain: The treaty was signed on December 24, 1814, but news had not yet crossed the Atlantic.
questions.tip: Andrew Jackson's big win came after the peace: slow mail, famous battle.

questions.q: In which year did the Spanish-American War take place?
questions.explain: The war lasted only a few months in 1898.
questions.tip: A 'splendid little war' in '98.

questions.q: In what year did the U.S. enter World War II?
questions.explain: The U.S. declared war on Japan on December 8, 1941; Germany and Italy declared war on the U.S. on December 11.
questions.tip: The war began in '39, America signed on in '41.

questions.q: When was the Korean War fought?
questions.explain: North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950; an armistice was signed in July 1953.
questions.tip: Korea: three years in the early '50s.

questions.q: The Persian Gulf War's Operation Desert Storm, to expel Iraq from Kuwait, took place in which year?
questions.explain: Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990; the U.S.-led coalition attacked in January and February 1991.
questions.tip: Desert Storm blew through in early '91.

questions.q: How long did the Hundred Years' War between England and France actually last?
questions.explain: It ran from 1337 to 1453, with long pauses. Joan of Arc fought in it.
questions.tip: The Hundred Years' War went into overtime: 116 years.

questions.q: When was the Thirty Years' War fought?
questions.explain: It began with the Defenestration of Prague and ended with the Peace of Westphalia.
questions.tip: Prague tossed men out a window in 1618, and Westphalia closed it in 1648.

questions.q: When was the Mexican-American War fought?
questions.explain: It followed the U.S. annexation of Texas and ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
questions.tip: '46 to '48, and the Gold Rush followed right after.

questions.q: When did U.S. combat involvement in Vietnam effectively end with the Paris Peace Accords?
questions.explain: U.S. combat troops withdrew in 1973; Saigon fell to North Vietnam in 1975.
questions.tip: U.S. out in '73, Saigon fell in '75.

questions.q: What does the 5th Amendment protect, among other things?
choices: The right not to testify against yourself
The right to a speedy trial
questions.explain: It also protects against double jeopardy and guarantees due process.
questions.tip: 'Pleading the Fifth' means you won't testify against yourself.

questions.q: What did the 14th Amendment (1868) establish?
choices: Birthright citizenship and equal protection of the laws
questions.explain: It is the basis of many landmark civil rights decisions, including Brown v. Board.
questions.tip: 13 freed, 14 made citizens equal, 15 gave the vote.

questions.q: The 15th Amendment (1870) prohibited denying the right to vote based on what?
choices: Race, color or previous condition of servitude
Failure to pay a poll tax
questions.explain: In practice, many Southern states evaded it with poll taxes and literacy tests until the 1960s.
questions.tip: 15: the vote regardless of race.

questions.q: Which amendment lowered the voting age to 18?
questions.explain: Ratified in 1971, it was driven partly by the argument that 18-year-olds could be drafted for Vietnam.
questions.tip: Old enough to fight, old enough to vote: the 26th.

questions.q: What does the 22nd Amendment do?
choices: Limits presidents to two elected terms
questions.explain: Ratified in 1951 after FDR's four elections.
questions.tip: 22: two terms, too many after that.

questions.q: What does the 25th Amendment address?
questions.explain: Ratified in 1967 after JFK's assassination, it clarifies what happens when a president dies, resigns or cannot serve.
questions.tip: 25 is a quarter of 100: a plan if the President can't serve the whole term.

questions.q: What did the 17th Amendment (1913) change?
choices: Senators are elected directly by voters
questions.explain: Before 1913, state legislatures chose U.S. senators.
questions.tip: 16 taxed income, 17 let the people pick senators: both in 1913.

questions.q: The 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act did what?
choices: Banned Chinese laborers from immigrating to the U.S.
questions.explain: It was the first major U.S. law to bar immigration by a specific nationality; it was repealed in 1943.
questions.tip: 1882 shut the door; 1943 opened it a crack.

questions.q: What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 do?
choices: Banned literacy tests and added federal oversight of voting
questions.explain: Black voter registration in the South rose dramatically within a few years.
questions.tip: 1964 opened doors, 1965 opened ballot boxes.

questions.q: The Americans with Disabilities Act was signed in which year?
questions.explain: Signed by George H. W. Bush, it bans discrimination based on disability.
questions.tip: ADA in 1990: ramps and rights for all.

questions.q: What did the Homestead Act of 1862 offer?
choices: 160 acres of public land to settlers who farmed it for five years
questions.explain: It helped settle the Great Plains, largely at the expense of Native nations.
questions.tip: Home-stead: make a home, get the land.

questions.q: Who was the Supreme Allied Commander for the D-Day invasion?
questions.explain: Eisenhower later served two terms as President, from 1953 to 1961.
questions.tip: Ike led the landing, then led the land.

questions.q: Who was the U.S. President during World War I?
questions.explain: Wilson won reelection in 1916 partly on the slogan 'He kept us out of war'.
questions.tip: Wilson in WWI: W and W.

questions.q: Which President made the decision to use atomic bombs on Japan?
questions.explain: FDR died in April 1945, and Truman became President only months before the bombings.
questions.tip: The buck stopped with Truman.

questions.q: Who was the Soviet leader during World War II?
questions.explain: Stalin ruled from the late 1920s until his death in 1953.
questions.tip: Lenin started the USSR; Stalin steered it through the war.

questions.q: Who became British Prime Minister in May 1940 and led Britain through most of WWII?
questions.explain: Churchill replaced Chamberlain, whose appeasement policy had failed.
questions.tip: Chamberlain appeased, Churchill wouldn't cease.

questions.q: Who was the Soviet leader during the Cuban Missile Crisis?
questions.explain: Khrushchev and Kennedy negotiated the removal of Soviet missiles from Cuba.
questions.tip: Kennedy and Khrushchev: the K-K standoff.

questions.q: Which President signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
questions.explain: Kennedy proposed it in 1963, and Johnson pushed it through Congress after Kennedy's assassination.
questions.tip: LBJ signed it in '64, then voting rights in '65.

questions.q: Who said 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' in 1987?
questions.explain: Reagan spoke at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin.
questions.tip: Reagan's request came true two years later.

questions.q: Who was the last leader of the Soviet Union?
questions.explain: His reforms, glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), helped bring about the USSR's end.
questions.tip: Gorbachev: glasnost, perestroika and goodbye USSR.

questions.q: Which President oversaw the start of construction of the Panama Canal by the U.S.?
questions.explain: Roosevelt backed Panama's independence from Colombia in 1903 to secure the canal zone.
questions.tip: Teddy dug big: the canal was his pride.

questions.q: Who was President during the War of 1812?
questions.explain: Dolley Madison famously helped save a portrait of George Washington as the British approached the White House.
questions.tip: Madison was mad at Britain in 1812.

questions.q: Who was President when the Louisiana Purchase was made?
questions.explain: Jefferson worried the Constitution did not explicitly allow buying land, but went ahead.
questions.tip: Jefferson's bargain: about 3 cents an acre.

questions.q: Which 1803 case established the Supreme Court's power of judicial review?
questions.explain: Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that courts can strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution.
questions.tip: Marbury made the Court mighty.

questions.q: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) held that...
choices: Congress has implied powers, and states cannot tax a federal bank
questions.explain: Marshall wrote that 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy'.
questions.tip: McCulloch: the bank stays, and Maryland pays nothing.

questions.q: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) concerned which federal power?
questions.explain: The case involved steamboat licenses on New York waters and broadly defined commerce.
questions.tip: Steamboats steered the Commerce Clause.

questions.q: The Dred Scott decision of 1857 ruled what?
choices: Black Americans could not be citizens, and Congress could not ban slavery in territories
questions.explain: The ruling inflamed sectional tensions and was overturned by the 13th and 14th Amendments.
questions.tip: One of the worst rulings ever, and it pushed the nation toward war.

questions.q: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) guaranteed what right?
choices: A lawyer for criminal defendants who cannot afford one
questions.explain: Clarence Gideon wrote his petition by hand from a Florida prison.
questions.tip: Gideon got a lawyer for everyone.

questions.q: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) led to which police practice?
choices: Warning suspects of their right to remain silent and to an attorney
questions.explain: The 'Miranda warning' begins 'You have the right to remain silent'.
questions.tip: If you've watched a cop show, you've heard Miranda.

questions.q: Korematsu v. United States (1944) upheld what?
choices: The wartime internment of Japanese Americans
questions.explain: The decision is widely condemned today, and the Court formally repudiated it in 2018.
questions.tip: Korematsu: a ruling the Court itself later regretted.

questions.q: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected students' rights to do what?
choices: Wear black armbands to protest the Vietnam War
questions.explain: The Court said students do not 'shed their constitutional rights... at the schoolhouse gate'.
questions.tip: Tinker's armbands: free speech goes to school too.

questions.q: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) set which standard for public officials suing for libel?
questions.explain: Officials must show a false statement was made knowing it was false or with reckless disregard for the truth.
questions.tip: To win, show the paper lied on purpose: actual malice.

questions.q: Who argued Brown v. Board of Education before the Supreme Court for the NAACP?
questions.explain: Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the unanimous opinion; Marshall later joined the Court himself.
questions.tip: Marshall argued it, Warren wrote it.

questions.q: In 732, Charles Martel halted an Umayyad advance into France at which battle?
questions.explain: The battle is often seen as limiting Umayyad expansion into Western Europe; Martel was Charlemagne's grandfather.
questions.tip: Martel means hammer: Charles hammered at Tours.

questions.q: In 1492, besides Columbus's voyage, what happened in Spain?
questions.explain: Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada in January 1492 and expelled Spain's Jews later that year.
questions.tip: 1492 was a busy year for Ferdinand and Isabella.

questions.q: In which year was the Spanish Armada defeated by England?
questions.explain: Elizabeth I's navy and stormy weather wrecked Philip II's invasion fleet.
questions.tip: Elizabeth beat Philip in '88, and storms finished the job.

questions.q: The Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC is famous for a stand by 300 soldiers from which city-state?
questions.explain: King Leonidas and his Spartans, with other Greek allies, held a narrow pass against the Persian army of Xerxes.
questions.tip: 300 Spartans at the hot gates: Thermopylae means hot gates.

questions.q: The First Opium War (1839 to 1842) was fought between China and which country?
questions.explain: Britain fought to keep selling opium in China and won Hong Kong in the peace treaty.
questions.tip: Britain's opium, China's loss of Hong Kong.

questions.q: The 1994 genocide in which country killed hundreds of thousands of Tutsi in about 100 days?
questions.explain: Hutu extremists carried out the killings from April to July 1994.
questions.tip: Rwanda, 1994: 100 days the world must remember.

questions.q: The Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, ruled which country from 1975 to 1979?
questions.explain: Its brutal policies caused the deaths of an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people.
questions.tip: Khmer is the main people and language of Cambodia.

questions.q: Which war (1853 to 1856) is remembered for Florence Nightingale and the Charge of the Light Brigade?
questions.explain: Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire fought Russia.
questions.tip: Nightingale's lamp lit up the Crimea.

questions.q: German unification in 1871 was engineered largely by which Prussian leader?
questions.explain: Bismarck used wars against Denmark, Austria and France to unite the German states.
questions.tip: Bismarck's 'blood and iron' forged Germany.

questions.q: Italian unification in the 1800s is known by which name?
questions.explain: Leaders included Cavour, Garibaldi and Mazzini; Rome became the capital in 1871.
questions.tip: Risorgimento means resurgence: Italy rising again.

questions.q: Teaching at the University of Oxford began before the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded.
questions.explain: Teaching at Oxford existed by 1096; Tenochtitlan was founded around 1325.
questions.tip: Some 'medieval' things are older than some 'ancient' ones.

questions.q: The Battle of Lepanto in 1571 was a major naval defeat for which empire?
questions.explain: A Holy League fleet led by Spain and Venice defeated the Ottoman navy in the Mediterranean.
questions.tip: Lepanto: the Ottoman fleet's big oops in the Med.
